title: A call from the press
stem:
You are an F2 doctor in the Emergency Department. A well-known television presenter has just been brought in after a car crash.

You answer the department phone, and the caller says she is a journalist. She asks whether the presenter is in the department and how badly hurt he is.
instruction: Choose the 3 most appropriate actions to take in this situation.

options.text: Confirm he is in the department, but say you can't give details.
options.brief: Confirming his presence is itself a breach of confidentiality.
options.detailed: This feels like a careful compromise, but simply confirming that he is a patient discloses confidential information.

options.text: Tell her he is stable, so that inaccurate reports aren't published.
options.detailed: Concern about inaccurate reporting is understandable, but you can't share information about him without his consent.

options.text: Tell her you can't confirm or deny whether anyone is a patient.
options.brief: Even confirming his presence would breach his confidentiality.
options.detailed: Whether someone is in hospital is confidential information. Declining to confirm or deny, politely, protects him without giving anything away.

options.text: Ask the presenter whether he would like you to talk to the journalist.
options.brief: Not your role, and he is injured and in the middle of assessment.
options.detailed: His wishes do matter, and the communications team will ask him. But approaching him yourself, while he is being assessed after a crash, isn't appropriate.

options.text: Direct her to the trust's communications team.
options.brief: Media enquiries should go through the press office.
options.detailed: Trusts have communications teams to handle media enquiries, with the patient's agreement. Referring her there is the proper route.

options.text: Let the nurse in charge know about the call.
options.brief: The department may need to prepare for more enquiries.
options.detailed: A call from the press suggests more may follow. The nurse in charge can alert the communications team and make sure staff are prepared.

options.text: Take her number and promise to call back with an update.
options.brief: Implies that information will be shared.
options.detailed: This suggests you will give her information later, which you can't do.

options.text: Mention to colleagues that he is in the department so they're prepared.
options.detailed: Only staff involved in his care need to know he is there. Telling others unnecessarily increases the risk of a leak.

explanation.issue: This tests whether you protect a patient's confidentiality when the media ask about him.
explanation.keyDetails: The caller is a journalist. The patient is well known. Even his presence is confidential.
explanation.reasoning: [C] protects his confidentiality, [E] uses the proper route, and [F] prepares the department. The distractors disclose information ([A], [B], [H]), or act outside your role ([D], [G]).
explanation.competing: [A] is the tempting option, but confirming his presence is a disclosure in itself.

references.title: Confidentiality: good practice in handling patient information
references.note: Not disclosing information about patients, including whether they are patients, without consent.
